turns.input: Begin the story.
turns.output:
The Academy primer devotes eleven pages to precedence and exactly one sentence to tonight:

*The first-year welcome table observes the custom of its residence.*

On the desk, the sentence looks almost smug beneath the lamp.

Garvey House offers no clarification. Voices rise through the floorboards—chairs shifting, silverware being counted, someone objecting that the centerpiece is “an armed shrub.” Warm air carries rosemary, baked pears, and woodsmoke up the central stair.

Your carefully mended coat is the only garment in the room that wasn’t selected by the Garvey lawyers. The inherited signet catches the light on your hand. Across from the bed, a framed old letter promises some long-dead woman’s great-nephew that his room will be ready when he visits. He evidently never did.

Beyond the window, the Academy gardens descend in pale terraces toward the plateau’s edge. One of the six bridges burns across the dark as a narrow road of hard white light. Far below it, lightning spreads soundlessly through the perpetual storm.

A brass chime rings downstairs.

Your door, which has been drifting open on an unreliable latch, admits a wedge of brighter hallway light. Footsteps approach and stop short of the threshold.

A young woman stands there in white and gold. Warm light rests beneath her skin, gentler than the lamps, and two small white wings sit folded behind her shoulders. Her blue eyes flick from the signet to the open primer.

“You must be Rowan Garvey. The signet makes that clear.  
I’m Seraphel Dawnquill; the dining hall is near.

“If you’re waiting for a rule that tells you when to go,  
The bell downstairs is all the rule I know.”

She remains in the hall, giving your room its boundary.

“Would you like some company when you walk through the door?  
They may stare a little less if they’ve seen me before.”

turns.input: I go down to dinner, introduce myself as Rowan, and take an available place at the table.
turns.output:
You accompany Seraphel down the main stair. It curves through the common room, where firelight shines on the varnished faces of dead Garveys. A lacquered deck of cards and four empty glasses wait on one low table; books, practice gloves, and an abandoned teacup occupy another. The house already bears the disorder of people living in it.

The dining-hall conversation thins when you enter.

All seventeen places have been set, though only seven are occupied. Candles double themselves in the polished table, and an arrangement of silver-leafed thornvine leans noticeably toward the heat of a tall, ember-skinned woman midway down the table. Beside her sits a brown-skinned man in an immaculate coat, fine dark fur visible across the backs of his hands.

He rises first.

“Rashid vel Amara. Welcome to Garvey House.” His amber eyes briefly take in the signet. “The name on the door doesn’t make you responsible for finding anything. None of us knows where they keep the salt.”

“Top cabinet beside the serving hatch,” says the horned woman.

Rashid looks at her. “You knew this entire time.”

“I looked.”

A corner of her mouth lifts. Her long tail has been tucked around the legs of her chair to keep it clear of the servers.

You introduce yourself simply. “I’m Rowan.”

“Everyone suspected,” says a pale-gold woman with elaborately arranged silver hair. One pointed ear angles toward you. “Caelindra Vaeyn.”

The snow-pale woman beside her sets down a goblet beaded with condensation. The water inside has begun to film with ice. “Ysolde Thornmantle.”

“Ashara vel Kothren,” says the horned woman.

At the far side of the table, a golden-haired man in formal white inclines his head. “Aldric Verantus. The return of a Garvey to the Conclave is an event of great significance.”

“It’s also dinner,” Ashara says.

Aldric’s expression tightens. “Those statements aren’t in conflict.”

“No, but only one is getting cold.”

The nearest open place is beside a slight woman whose skin carries a pale green cast. Her entirely black eyes follow the movement of the chair as you draw it back, and her blue-black hair drifts against her shoulders despite the still air.

“Thessaly Morrow,” she says. She moves a bread plate clear of your sleeve. “That place is free. The napkin belongs to the Academy, apparently. They count them.”

Seraphel takes the chair on your other side.

“Eight names at once tend to vanish through the floor;  
By pudding you’ll know five of us, and breakfast may bring more.”

A server places bowls of dark onion broth around the table. The thornvine bends farther toward Ashara and hooks one silver barb into Rashid’s cuff.

Caelindra watches it happen. “It has attacked a Conclave heir within six minutes. I maintain that it is an unsuitable centerpiece.”

“It only caught the cloth,” Rashid says, carefully freeing the fabric. “Its political judgment may be sound.”

Ashara laughs outright. Ysolde reaches across, pours a little water into the centerpiece’s dry basin, and turns it away from the demon’s heat. The vine slowly relaxes.

“It was thirsty,” she says.

For several minutes, the room settles into the practical sounds of dinner: spoons against porcelain, servers replacing bread, the low hiss of a lamp being adjusted. No one bows to you. No one asks you to claim the empty head of the table beneath the largest Garvey portrait.

Caelindra’s gaze pauses on the ink along your fingers. Rashid notices the carefully repaired seam at your cuff. Ashara looks from both to your inherited ring.

“The verification notice says you inherited a name,” she says. “It says very little about the life you had before it. What did you do?”

turns.input: I say, "Most recently I earned my keep copying books. I haven't had much practice at being an heir." I help myself to dinner.
turns.output:
“Most recently I earned my keep copying books,” you say. “I haven’t had much practice at being an heir.”

You help yourself from the dishes within reach: hot brown bread, roast onions glazed with honey, and slices of herb-crusted bird. The serving fork is dragon-made, heavy enough to be a minor weapon.

Ashara looks from your ink-stained fingers to the signet.

“Most heirs practice in private for years before they’re allowed to make mistakes in public,” she says. “You’ll be doing both at once.”

“What she means,” Rashid says, “is that no one arrives prepared.”

“I meant what I said.”

“Yes. That’s generally the difficulty.”

Ashara gives him a level look, then returns to her meal. Her tail nudges his chair leg once beneath the table. Rashid moves the chair half an inch without looking down.

Aldric folds his hands beside his bowl. “The Conclave track is designed to supply what prior circumstances could not. Law, diplomacy, history, moral formation.”

“Duelling,” Ashara adds.

“Duelling is not moral formation.”

“That depends on the instructor.”

The dark bread has a crisp salt crust. The onions carry enough pepper to make the air above Ashara’s plate shimmer more strongly when she exhales. Beside you, Thessaly disassembles a pastry into exact layers, eating the sugared fruit and leaving the crust arranged in a neat spiral.

Caelindra has not resumed eating. Her gaze rests on the ink worked into the creases of your fingertips.

“A competent copyist is more useful than an incompetent heir,” she says. “Though the pay is usually reversed.”

Rashid lifts his glass slightly in agreement. “Accurate books are one of the few things everyone claims to value and no one budgets for.”

“They budget for decoration,” Caelindra says. “I once received a botanical compendium with eighty-seven hand-painted borders and the same poisonous mushroom labeled as edible on four separate pages.”

Ysolde cuts a thin piece from the chilled, nearly raw meat on her plate. “Was anyone harmed.”

“No. My mother sent it to an aunt.”

A brief silence follows.

Caelindra’s pointed ears shift backward. “The error was found before she used it.”

Ashara covers a laugh with her cup. Even Aldric’s mouth twitches.

Seraphel breaks her bread and says,

“A murderous mushroom makes scholarship exciting;  
Though less for the reader who trusts what you’re writing.”

“That is precisely why copying matters,” Caelindra says. She turns her violet eyes back to your stained fingers rather than the inherited ring. “What sort of books did people pay you to copy?”

turns.input: I eat and listen to the conversation around me, without trying to take charge of it.
turns.output:
Caelindra waits for an answer, but she doesn’t repeat the question. When none comes, she returns to her dinner, occasionally glancing at the ink on your hands.

Conversation moves on without requiring you to move it.

Rashid reminds Ashara that her opponent in tomorrow’s ranked bout has changed his declared weapon from spear to paired blades.

“He wants me preparing for paired blades,” Ashara says.

“He may simply prefer paired blades.”

“That would be disappointingly straightforward.”

Ysolde lifts her eyes from her chilled meat. “The wind will turn east tomorrow. The octagon’s western edge will be difficult for anyone with wings.”

Aldric’s shoulders draw subtly straighter beneath his white-and-gold robes. “The rankings ought to test discipline, not accidents of weather.”

“The weather is present whether you approve of it or not,” Ysolde says.

Thessaly eats another sugared layer from her pastry. “So is Ashara.”

Ashara laughs, and the table loosens around the sound.

The meal continues through spiced roots, soft white cheese, and pears baked until their skins split in the syrup. No one asks you to account for humanity, defend your inheritance, or pronounce on Council law. Rashid and Caelindra argue over whether a mistranslated treaty is still binding. Ysolde contributes one sentence about a border accord that spent forty years buried beneath an avalanche. Seraphel listens while quietly tapping a rhythm against her cup.

As the last pear disappears from Ashara’s plate, a woman’s voice carries in from the common room.

“Amara, this house owns seventeen kinds of fork and no corkscrew.”

Rashid stops with his cup halfway to his mouth.

A compact demon woman appears in the doorway. One short horn bears a brass cap, and her right wrist is confined in a dark leather splint. Two other students wait behind her, one carrying bottles and the other a wooden case of cards.

The injured woman looks at the cleared dessert dishes. “Also, you’re late.”

“Dinner has not formally ended,” Rashid says.

“The pears are gone. That’s an ending.”

Ashara looks between them. “Dena.”

“Vel Kothren.” Dena’s attention returns to Rashid. “The cards are set up.”

Rashid places his cup down with great precision. “Start without me. I’ll join you after drills.”

Dena’s eyes shift to Ashara, then to the wrapped practice blades resting beside her chair.

“You scheduled drills.”

“I expected the three of you could begin.”

“We can begin. We could also have stayed in Commerce House and begun.” She adjusts the splint against her chest. “We came because you said you’d spend the first half-hour with us.”

Rashid’s courtesy becomes noticeably more exact. “I said I would.”

“Yesterday,” Dena says. “Before you agreed to this.”

Ashara turns her gold eyes on him. “You accepted my invitation this afternoon.”

“Yes.”

“And neglected to mention that you’d already promised someone else.”

“I thought you needed a partner who knew your habits more than they needed a fourth player.”

Dena’s mouth flattens. “You decided what I needed again.”

Rashid draws breath, but she continues.

“This isn’t a meeting about the practice group. I told you I don’t want one. I wanted cards, bad wine, and an evening in which no one uses my wrist to launch a campaign.”

The two students behind her study the ceiling with practiced concentration.

Rashid looks down at the table. When he answers, the polish remains, but the argument has gone out of it. “You did tell me. I’m sorry.”

Ashara pushes back her chair. “Go play cards.”

“I can give you twenty minutes first.”

“I asked for thirty.”

“Then I’ll—”

“No. You made the first promise to them.” She picks up her practice blades. “I’ll drill footwork alone. Tomorrow, sixth bell, you give me the half-hour you owe me.”

Rashid nods once. “Agreed.”

Dena doesn’t smile at winning. She steps aside to let him pass, and the four of them move into the common room. A moment later comes the snap of cards being shuffled and Dena saying, “If you organize us into teams, I’m leaving.”

Thessaly rises with her unfinished pastry and follows at a measured distance toward the game. Aldric departs for evening prayer. Ysolde opens the garden door, admitting a ribbon of cold air, while Caelindra gathers a book she had left beneath her chair.

Ashara carries her practice blades toward the quadrangle alone.

The welcome dinner ends not with a ceremony, but with the house dividing into its separate evening pursuits around you.

turns.input: I stay at the table long enough to finish my food and hear what the others are planning for the evening.
turns.output:
You remain while the table empties around you. A server clears the abandoned settings but leaves your plate untouched, replacing your water and moving on without comment.

At the open garden door, Ysolde studies the darkness beyond the pale paths. Cold air settles around her boots.

“I’ll be in the lower garden until the wind turns,” she says. “The storm front should reach the eastern bridge before ninth bell.”

She steps outside. Her white hair remains visible for several moments, then passes behind a hedge.

Caelindra tucks her book beneath one arm. “I’m taking the west alcove in the library. Professor Windwhisper assigned the opening Accord commentary for tomorrow, and the common room has ceased to be suitable for reading.”

From that room comes the slap of a card against wood and Dena declaring, “That is the third rule you’ve remembered after dealing.”

“It was always a rule,” Rashid says.

“It becomes less convincing each time.”

Thessaly still stands near their table with her pastry plate. Dena shifts a chair out with one foot.

“Morrow, sit down if you’re staying. We’ll teach you.”

“I don’t know the game.”

“That’s why we’ll teach you.”

Thessaly takes the offered chair. Rashid begins laying out the cards more slowly, naming each suit once. Dena stops him when he starts explaining strategy.

Seraphel rises beside you, collecting several loose pages from beneath her place setting.

“I’ll take the high gallery, well out of sight;  
The choir wants these verses by tomorrow night.”

Caelindra glances at the pages. “Tap the rhythm quietly. That railing carries sound through the entire library.”

Seraphel presses a hand to her chest in exaggerated innocence, then follows her through the library door without making any promise.

The distant chapel bell marks the hour; Aldric is already gone in that direction. Through the dining-hall windows, a tall ember-red figure crosses the lamplit quadrangle toward the octagon, practice blades over one shoulder.

You finish the last of your meal as the house settles into separate pockets of activity. Cards and low argument occupy the common room. Lamplight climbs the library’s iron stair. The garden door remains open to the cold, and beyond the glass Ashara disappears along the path to the dueling ground.

A server removes your empty plate. For the moment, no one requires anything from you.

turns.input: If Ashara is still nearby, I ask whether an untrained partner would be any use for practice. If she has already left, I let the opportunity pass.
turns.output:
When you look through the dining-hall windows again, the quadrangle is empty. Ashara has already passed beneath the low dragon-carved arch and taken the descending path toward the octagon. Reaching her now would mean following rather than catching her nearby.

You leave the offer unsaid.

A short while later, the first crack of a wooden practice blade carries faintly from the dueling ground. Another follows, then a measured sequence as Ashara begins her footwork drills alone.

Behind you, a server extinguishes the dining candles one by one. The common room remains warm and noisy with cards; the library door is shut, a thin line of lamplight beneath it. Cold air continues through the open garden door.

Your unasked question remains unknown to Ashara, and the opportunity passes without consequence.

turns.input: I accept whatever answer she has given and leave her plans alone. I finish my meal rather than following anyone to practice.
turns.output:
No answer comes; the question never reaches Ashara. You leave her to the drills she has already begun.

Your plate is empty, and the last serving dishes have been carried away. A server snuffs the candles nearest the vacant head of the table.

“Breakfast begins at seventh bell, Mr. Garvey. The common room remains open through the night.”

He withdraws with the final tray.

From beyond the wall comes Dena’s delighted accusation that Thessaly has learned the game suspiciously quickly. In the distance, Ashara’s practice blade continues its steady cadence, already too far away for conversation.

The dining hall settles into darkness behind you, its welcome dinner concluded.

turns.input: I go to the house library and look on the open shelves for an introductory book about the Council. If I need help finding one, I ask whoever is working there.
turns.output:
The library opens directly from the dining hall. Its air smells of lamp oil, old leather, and dust warmed by enclosed flames. An iron stair coils to the gallery above.

Caelindra has claimed the west alcove as promised. Three books lie open around her, held flat by polished stones. She glances up when you enter, then returns to her reading without renewing her earlier question.

On the upper gallery, Seraphel sits among loose sheets of music, tapping a quiet rhythm against the rail.

The open shelves are labeled with brass plaques: *Founding Commentary*, *Delegated Powers*, *Council Proceedings*, *Covenant Law*. Nothing admits to being introductory. Most of the likely volumes begin with a numeral greater than one or a title assuming familiarity with three prior controversies.

An elderly human man works at the central desk, spectacles low on his nose. Grey threads run through his cropped hair, and old ink marks the sides of two fingers. He is sorting catalogue cards into narrow wooden drawers.

You approach him. “I’m looking for an introductory book about the Council.”

He studies the shelves you have been searching, not you.

“Those are arranged for the convenience of people who already know where everything is.” He rises. “Procedure is this way.”

He leads you past the spiral stair to a low shelf partly concealed by a reading stand. From it he removes a thick blue volume with softened corners: *The Council in Practice: Seats, Petitions, Votes, and Powers*.

“This is current through last year. It explains what the Council does before attempting to justify why.” He brushes dust from the title. “Its account of weighted votes is the Academy’s preferred argument, not the only argument. Keep that distinction in mind.”

He offers you the book.

“Gareth Stone. I teach human Covenant history.” His eyes touch the Garvey signet, but he asks nothing about it. “Open-shelf books may stay down here until midnight. Use the ledger if you take one to your room.”

Professor Stone returns to his catalogue cards. Caelindra continues reading in the west alcove, and Seraphel’s measured tapping travels softly through the iron stair.

An empty table stands beneath a green-shaded lamp, the introductory volume now in your hands.

turns.input: Once I have a book, I settle down and read quietly for half an hour.
turns.output:
You take the blue volume to the empty table and settle beneath the green lamp.

The book has been copied by several hands. The first is broad and careful; later chapters grow smaller and more crowded where a second copyist tried to preserve the original page count. Its opening diagram shows seven seats around a circular chamber. The human seat is shaded grey and labeled *dormant*, the terminology current before your inheritance was verified.

The first chapter separates titles that ordinary speech treats as interchangeable. A Council representative may vote and bind their government. A designated heir may observe, advise when recognized, and act under expressly delegated authority. A Conclave student possesses access and standing, but no independent power to commit anyone—not even their own house.

The procedural sections are dry but clear. Petitions enter through individual seats. Treaty disputes go first to arbitration panels drawn from uninvolved delegations. Certain motions require support across several races before they can even be debated. Empty seats retain their legal existence; their authority cannot simply be divided among those remaining.

Stone’s warning becomes evident in the chapter on voting. The book describes restrictions on the beastkin seat as “transitional safeguards,” though the accompanying dates show that the transition has lasted generations. Angel-sponsored precedents appear as foundational examples. Demon objections are generally confined to footnotes.

The human vacancy receives two pages. According to the official account, demographic collapse made a functioning delegation impossible. The Council therefore placed human privileges in abeyance while leaving its treaties and obligations intact. The book offers no procedure for what happens when a verified heir reappears after sixty years. It directs such “unlikely contingencies” to the Covenant’s general succession provisions in a later volume.

Around you, the library remains quiet. Caelindra turns pages in the west alcove. Above, Seraphel marks corrections on her choir sheets without speaking. Professor Stone’s catalogue drawers open and close with soft wooden clicks.

Half an hour passes. When the library clock advances, you have reached the beginning of the chapter on committees, with a strip of paper resting between the pages to keep your place.

turns.input: As I read, I silently wonder whether my aunt once kept a blue glass bird on her desk. I do not say this aloud; it is only a private guess. I return my attention to the page.
turns.output:
For a moment, a private question crosses the printed lines: whether your aunt once kept a blue glass bird on her desk.

It remains only a guess. You give it no voice, and nothing in the library changes. Caelindra turns a page. Professor Stone closes another catalogue drawer. Seraphel’s pencil continues across the gallery above.

You return your attention to the book.

The committee chapter explains that most Council business is shaped before any public vote. Committees decide which petitions receive hearings, which require further translation, and which are returned without debate. Their chairs officially rotate among the seated delegations, though temporary extensions can last for years.

A dense table of offices and procedural limits fills the next page. You follow it line by line beneath the steady green lamp.

turns.input: I take a short break in the common room. If Seraphel is there and not occupied in a conversation, I ask, "What do you like reading for pleasure?" Otherwise I sit with my book.
turns.output:
You mark your place, close the blue volume, and carry it into the common room.

Seraphel is not there. Through the open library doorway, her loose pages remain spread across the upper gallery, and the faint scratch of her pencil continues overhead. Caelindra is still concealed in the west alcove.

The card game occupies a low table near the fireplace. Dena has propped her splinted wrist on a cushion while she plays with her other hand. Thessaly sits beside her, captured cards arranged in exact rows. Rashid and the two visiting students fill out the table.

Rashid acknowledges you with a nod but doesn’t draw you into the game. The half-hour he promised Dena has passed, yet he remains for another deal.

Their conversation has moved well away from injuries and practice groups. Dena is recounting the time Rashid gave a Commerce instructor a brass ruler for Midwinter.

“He used it to measure our assignment margins,” she says. “Then deducted marks from everyone whose lines were an eighth-inch too wide.”

“I was seventeen,” Rashid says. “The gift was sincere.”

“That made it funnier.”

Thessaly studies him across her cards. “You supplied the instrument of your own punishment.”

“Yes.”

She considers this, then plays a card that makes Dena laugh and costs Rashid most of his counters.

You settle into a deep leather chair at the edge of the firelight, the Council book resting closed across your knees. The room asks nothing of you. For several minutes there is only the warmth of the hearth, the soft slap of cards, and conversation continuing comfortably without your management.

turns.input: If we are talking, I ask Seraphel what she likes about her choice. If she has chosen not to talk, I let her be and read.
turns.output:
Seraphel remains in the library gallery, occupied with her choir pages. There is no conversation between you to continue, so you leave her to the work and open the blue volume again.

Firelight warms one edge of the pages as you read the section on speaking order. The book calls the order ceremonial, but places the beastkin delegation last in most general debates because it joined the Covenant later. Earlier speakers can define the terms of a motion before that seat is recognized.

The following pages describe the human delegation’s former administrative duties. Humans frequently chaired translation and arbitration panels, while magical disputes were sent to mixed committees under their supervision. After the human collapse, those duties were reassigned through a series of temporary orders. The vote itself remained dormant rather than passing to another seat.

At the card table, Thessaly wins another hand. Dena gathers the cards to deal again, and Rashid accepts the loss without trying to revise the rules.

No one interrupts your reading. Seraphel’s pencil continues faintly beyond the library door.

turns.input: I let the conversation end naturally and return to my book. I stay with it until I finish the chapter.
turns.output:
You don’t enter the card-table conversation. It winds down on its own as the final hand ends.

Dena gathers her winnings with her uninjured hand. “That’s enough. I have Commerce at eighth bell.”

The two visiting students begin collecting the empty glasses. Rashid closes the card case without attempting to arrange anyone’s morning.

“We play again next week,” Dena tells Thessaly. “You’re welcome.”

“I’d like that,” Thessaly says.

They leave without turning the evening into a meeting about Dena’s wrist. Rashid remains by the dying fire, stacking cushions and clearing one spilled drink, while Thessaly carries her pastry plate toward the kitchen.

You continue reading.

The last portion of the chapter concerns committee reports. A majority report advances automatically to the Council agenda; a dissenting seat may append objections, but must secure another delegation’s support to force separate debate. Emergency administrative orders can be renewed by committee rather than by the full Council, provided they do not formally alter the rights of a seat.

A table lists the orders renewed since the human vacancy. Translation work, arbitration scheduling, and oversight of mixed magical disputes have all remained under “temporary” arrangements for decades. The book presents this as proof that the institution can continue functioning through a prolonged absence.

The chapter ends with a concise diagram tracing a petition from submission to final vote. You follow the arrows through review, translation, committee hearing, and scheduling until the text reaches its heavy dividing line.

Beyond it, the next heading reads: *Succession, Recognition, and Vacant Seats.*

You have finished the chapter. Around you, the common room has grown quieter, the fire reduced to a red bed of coals.

turns.input: I go to bed when I am done reading. The next morning I wash, dress, and get breakfast in time for the scheduled orientation.
turns.output:
You return the Council volume to the library’s central desk, then climb to the second floor. The house quiets by degrees beneath you: doors closing, pipes knocking in the walls, the common-room fire being banked for the night.

No one disturbs you before morning.

The seventh bell sounds while grey light spreads across the gardens. You wash with cold water from the basin, dress in a clean shirt and your mended charcoal coat, and secure the Garvey signet on your hand. Water does little to discipline your hair.

Breakfast is less formal than dinner. The long table has been left bare, with porridge, eggs, bread, fruit, and tea arranged on a sideboard. You fill a plate and eat without being delayed.

Ashara and Rashid arrive from their rescheduled sixth-bell practice carrying wooden blades and streaked with octagon dust. Ashara’s heat lifts faint steam from her shoulders. Rashid’s immaculate appearance has finally suffered: one cuff is untucked, and grit marks a knee. They speak quietly over their food about the bout later today, neither mentioning last night’s dispute.

Aldric has already returned from dawn prayer. Caelindra reads beside her breakfast, holding the pages clear of the honey. Thessaly appears last, accepts a cup of tea, and sits in companionable silence near Rashid.

You finish with enough time to cross the quadrangle before the eighth bell. Morning light lays sharp divisions across its black demon stone, white angel marble, and living elven beams. Beneath the plateau, slow lightning moves through the storm without sound.

The Conclave seminar room holds fifteen chairs around an oval table, though only eight folders have been placed. Each bears a student’s name. Yours waits on the near curve beneath the framed Accords, their seven scripts running side by side.

At the head of the table, Professor Elara Windwhisper arranges a narrow stack of papers. Her name matches the orientation schedule. A young demon professor stands near the blackboard, reading the room as the other students take their places.

The eighth bell begins to ring just as you sit down. Professor Windwhisper closes the final folder and looks around the table.

turns.input: At orientation, I ask how a student in the human seat is supposed to learn the practical duties of the role.
turns.output:
The eighth bell fades. Professor Windwhisper introduces the young demon beside the blackboard as Professor Kira vel Shaan, instructor in Practical Rhetoric. Then she begins reviewing the folders: conduct rules, seminar schedules, committee simulations, and the conditions under which Conclave students may observe official proceedings.

When she pauses, you ask, “How is a student in the human seat supposed to learn the practical duties of the role?”

Windwhisper rests one hand on the table.

“A distinction first, Mr. Garvey. You are the recognized heir to the human seat and a Conclave student. You do not yet hold the Council seat or possess its authority.”

Her correction is quiet and matter-of-fact.

“Ordinarily, an heir learns through two institutions at once. The Academy teaches law and shared procedure. The incumbent delegation supplies staff work, supervised cases, and practical instruction during recess. The human delegation has neither an incumbent representative nor functioning staff.”

She draws a single sheet from her stack and passes it to Kira, who carries it around the table and places it before you.

The heading reads: *Provisional Curriculum for the Human Delegation.*

“For your first term,” Windwhisper continues, “each occupied delegation will provide a completed case with identifying details removed. You will reconstruct its handling under faculty supervision: translation, petition review, arbitration, committee preparation, and final recommendation. No single delegation will control your instruction.”

Rashid’s pen stops briefly over his notes. Ashara reads the sheet upside down from across the table but says nothing.

“In second term, you will observe open committee proceedings,” Windwhisper says. “Professor Stone’s course will address the historical human portfolio. It cannot replace an incumbent’s apprenticeship, but it will distinguish former human practice from duties redistributed during the vacancy. External placements will be decided after your first-year review.”

Kira leans one hip against the blackboard.

“The first practical case begins Monday. You’ll receive a petition, three witness accounts, two proposed remedies, and a translation bad enough to alter the dispute.” Her gold eyes move around the entire table rather than settling only on you. “Everyone submits a written recommendation. Everyone defends it aloud. That is where we begin.”

The provisional sheet supplies dates, supervisors, and the sequence of six delegation cases. Several later entries remain marked *pending cooperation*.

Windwhisper allows time for the room to read, then turns to the next item on the orientation schedule: rules for observing Council business without claiming authority you have not been delegated.

turns.input: I listen to the answer and then let the next person speak.
turns.output:
You leave the provisional curriculum on the table and listen.

Ashara speaks next. “Who chooses which completed cases the delegations submit?”

“Each delegation nominates a file,” Windwhisper says. “Faculty may accept it, reject it, or request a different one.”

“Then every office decides what it is willing to let us see.”

Kira answers from beside the blackboard. “Yes. That is why you are not graded on accepting the packet’s account of itself. Missing testimony, unexplained costs, convenient dates, and remedies no one could enforce all belong in your analysis.”

Ashara makes a brief note in her folder. Rashid does the same.

Windwhisper moves on to the rules governing simulations and observation. Conclave students may not invoke family authority during Academy exercises. They must identify themselves as students when corresponding with working delegations. Gifts, private briefings, and promises of future office must be disclosed to faculty.

Thessaly lifts one hand.

“Anything we sign during a simulation is legally void outside it.”

“All exercise documents are marked and countersigned as nonoperative,” Windwhisper confirms. “No simulation will create a debt, bargain, oath, or continuing obligation.”

Thessaly lowers her hand and returns to the printed rules.

The orientation proceeds through committee etiquette, travel permissions, and the process for requesting access to closed proceedings. No one directs another question at you. Windwhisper answers practical concerns precisely; Kira supplies examples drawn from failed negotiations and badly prepared petitions.

After forty minutes, Windwhisper closes her folder.

“Ten minutes. When you return, Professor Shaan will assign the opening exercise.”

Chairs shift around the oval table. Ashara rises to stretch the shoulder she trained that morning, while Rashid remains seated to finish copying a date from the board. The first portion of orientation ends without requiring anything further from you.

turns.input: After orientation I check the public dueling schedule. If I can watch Ashara's ranked bout, I take a place as a spectator; if it has already finished, I look at the posted result.
turns.output:
The second half of orientation consists of examples rather than speeches. Kira distributes a failed border petition and shows where its author assumed authority the office did not possess. Windwhisper reviews the first month’s schedule, including Monday’s written recommendation and a supervised committee simulation later in the week.

Orientation ends shortly after the tenth bell.

The public dueling board stands beside the path to the octagon. Today’s challenges have been written in chalk beneath the permanent rankings:

*Eleventh Bell — First Board*  
*Ashara vel Kothren, Rank One*  
*Merek Solane, Rank Three*  
*Declared weapons: single blade / paired blades*

A smaller note records Solane’s change from spear to paired blades yesterday afternoon. The bout has not begun.

You reach the dueling ground while the spectators are still gathering. Low stone terraces overlook the octagon’s packed earth, and you take an open place with a clear view. Streamers tied to the western posts pull steadily east in the changing wind.

Rashid stands near the front rail, his morning practice clothes replaced by another immaculate coat. Ysolde watches from the upper terrace, still enough that only her white hair moves in the wind. Neither draws you into conversation.

Ashara enters carrying one long wooden practice blade. She has retied her black hair, and the morning’s dust has been washed from her ember-red skin. Across from her, Merek Solane wears the white training coat of the Military track. At the referee’s signal, broad white wings manifest behind him. He draws two short practice blades whose warded edges shine gold.

The referee raises one hand.

“Three scoring contacts or a yield. Restricted force. Begin.”

Solane moves first. His wings drive him across the packed earth in a sudden low rush, one blade pressing Ashara’s guard outward while the other strikes her shoulder. Blue ward-light flashes across her coat.

“First touch, Solane.”

They reset.

Ashara gives ground during the second exchange, keeping her single blade between both of his. Solane attempts the same crossing attack. This time she steps inside it. Her hilt catches one wrist; the length of her blade turns and lands across his ribs.

“Second touch, vel Kothren.”

The third exchange lasts longer. Solane stays on the ground, using his wings to check and alter his momentum without committing to flight. His paired blades keep Ashara’s weapon occupied until a quick reversal reaches her side.

“Third touch, Solane. Two to one.”

The crowd shifts closer to the rail.

Ashara resets without looking toward the terraces. Heat rises visibly from her shoulders, wavering against the pale stone beyond her. When the referee begins the fourth exchange, she stops pursuing Solane’s retreats. She holds the center and makes him circle.

He moves toward the western edge. The east wind catches his open wings, forcing him to shorten one step. Ashara’s tail braces against the turn as she pivots. Her blade strikes the outside of his thigh before his second weapon can close.

“Fourth touch, vel Kothren. Two to two.”

For the final exchange, gold light runs along both of Solane’s blades. Ashara’s answering magic is smaller: a red flare beneath the skin of her sword arm, drawn inward rather than thrown.

Solane attacks from above. The wind pulls at one wing as he descends near the western boundary. Ashara slips under the first blade, takes the second against her guard, and turns the collision into a short strike against the center of his chest.

The ward on his coat flashes brilliant blue.

“Final touch, vel Kothren. Bout.”

Noise rolls across the terraces. Ashara lowers her weapon, breathing hard enough that steam lifts from her collar. Solane’s manifested wings fade. He presses a fist to his chest where the ward caught the blow, then offers her his forearm. She grips it once.

At the ranking board, an Academy clerk records the result without changing the order: Ashara remains first.

Spectators begin filing back toward the quadrangle. Ashara stays beside the octagon long enough to cool down and collect her practice gear, while Rashid waits near the rail.

turns.input: Afterward I spend an hour walking in the gardens on my own. I do not seek anyone out.
turns.output:
You leave the octagon with the dispersing spectators, then turn through the arched garden gate alone.

Pale walls break the plateau wind without shutting out the sky. Warm beds along the demon-stone foundations hold ember lilies and black-veined herbs; farther in, shaded pools keep frost flowers open beneath a skin of ice. Living elven arches bend over the path, their new leaves growing among others that have not fallen in decades.

The route loops gradually toward the plateau’s edge. There, a public terrace looks down on the perpetual storm. Slow lightning branches beneath your feet without thunder, illuminating the underside of one hard-light bridge as it reaches toward a distant territory.

You continue through narrower paths sheltered by high hedges. Water moves through dragon-carved channels cut low into the stone. Small brass plaques identify plants, their preferred climates, and several severe penalties for picking them.

Classes are still in session, and the paths remain largely empty. No one calls to you or alters your course. You walk until the next bell marks the hour, returning at last to the central garden gate with the circuit complete.

turns.input: I return to the common room. If Rashid is there and not busy, I ask how his evening went. Otherwise I leave him to it.
turns.output:
You return to Garvey House by the garden entrance. Midday light reaches across the common-room floor, catching dust above the cold fireplace.

Rashid sits alone at one of the study tables, winding fresh cord around the grip of a wooden practice blade. His coat hangs over the neighboring chair, and his sleeves are rolled above the dark fur on his forearms. When you enter, he finishes the loop he is tying and sets the blade down.

He doesn’t appear occupied, so you ask, “How did your evening go?”

“Better once I stopped trying to keep two promises at the same time.” He leans back. “Dena won two hands. Thessaly learned the game quickly enough that we accused her of prior experience. She truthfully denied it and continued taking our counters.”

A small smile shows one canine.

“We stayed well past the half-hour. No one discussed the practice group, Dena’s wrist, or anything useful. That was the point.” He glances at the newly wrapped grip. “Then Ashara collected every minute I owed her at sixth bell. At least the practice served its purpose.”

Rashid saw you reading the night before; his attention shifts briefly toward the library door.

“You had *The Council in Practice*. Did you reach its account of beastkin voting?”

turns.input: I settle down with my book again. I do not volunteer to sort out anyone else's arrangements.
turns.output:
You leave Rashid’s question unanswered. He waits a moment, then picks up the practice blade and resumes winding its grip without repeating himself.

The blue Council volume is back on its shelf in the adjoining library. You retrieve it, return to the common room, and settle into the leather chair near the cold fireplace.

The next chapter begins by separating inheritance from office. A family may designate or produce an heir according to its own laws, but that alone does not confer a Council vote. The Council verifies the claim, recognizes the successor’s standing, and eventually performs a formal investiture. Until then, an heir may study, observe, and exercise only authority specifically delegated in writing.

Another section states that a seat belongs to its signatory people rather than to whichever house currently supplies the representative. Family titles, property, and political office may pass together under ordinary circumstances, but the Covenant treats them as distinct grants of authority.

The examples are less useful. Every disputed succession described in the book involves a functioning government, an incumbent delegation, or rival houses able to submit competing claims. Its “extraordinary vacancies” last months or a few years, not generations.

The human seat appears only in a footnote:

*Current conditions remain subject to provisional recognition and Council review.*

No further procedure follows.

Across the room, Rashid finishes the new grip, tests it once against his palm, and leaves with the practice blade under one arm. He does not mention Dena, Ashara, or the unanswered question again.

You continue reading in the quiet he leaves behind.

turns.input: At the next communal meal I take an available seat. If Seraphel is there, I ask whether she knows a song worth learning; otherwise I listen to the table.
turns.output:
By the evening bell, the long dining table has been set for the eight first-years again. Tonight’s meal is less ceremonial: bowls of lamb stew, charred greens, warm bread, and a dark berry pudding waiting beneath silver covers.

You take an open chair across from Seraphel. Ink marks one cuff of her white-and-gold clothes, left from the choir work she carried into the library the night before.

Ashara is eating with the appetite of someone who has trained twice and fought a ranked bout. Rashid sits two places away, discussing Solane’s change of weapons with Ysolde. No one asks you to settle the disagreement over whether the east wind decided the final exchange.

When the bread has been passed, you ask Seraphel, “Do you know a song worth learning?”

She considers this while breaking her bread into the stew.

“*The Ferryman’s Coat* is worth learning to sing;  
It starts with a flood and concludes with a king.

“The melody’s simple, the chorus is strong;  
By third repetition, you’ll know the whole song.”

She taps the rhythm lightly against her bowl, then hums four bars under the table’s conversation. The tune moves at a walking pace, rises for the imagined chorus, and settles cleanly back on its opening note.

Caelindra looks up from her plate. “There are at least nineteen verses.”

Seraphel’s blue eyes brighten.

“Only six are required; the rest may be missed.  
The one with the turnips should never exist.”

That earns a quiet laugh from Rashid and a brief, unwilling smile from Aldric. Seraphel hums the chorus once more, without pressing you to sing along.

turns.input: I listen if someone wants to sing or explain the song, without supplying lyrics or a performance of my own. Otherwise I enjoy the meal.
turns.output:
Seraphel needs little encouragement. She sets down her spoon and explains the premise in the only manner her voice permits:

“The king takes his coat when the flood fills the square;  
The ferryman follows—his supper is there.”

Then she sings the chorus. Her voice is clear and warm, carrying easily without becoming a performance for the entire house.

“Pull for the quay while the black waters rise;  
The crown’s in the ferry, the court’s in disguise.

“The king has my coat and the cook has my oar;  
If anyone’s ruling, I’m not sure anymore.”

Rashid finds the rhythm against the table with two fingers. On the second repetition, Aldric adds a low harmony without looking up from his plate. He apparently knows a more formal version, but follows Seraphel’s melody instead.

Ashara joins only for the final line. Ysolde hums beneath it, so quietly that her version seems to move at a different tempo.

Caelindra listens with the expression of someone compiling objections. When the chorus ends, she says, “The cook disappears from the narrative after stealing the oar.”

Seraphel nods gravely.

“The sixth verse explains it, though poorly at best;  
He rows toward the palace and sinks with the rest.”

“That does not explain it.”

“It explains where he went.”

The berry pudding arrives before Caelindra can dispute the distinction. You eat and listen while Seraphel gives them two more verses, including one about a horse on a roof and another about the ferryman being mistaken for a minor duke.

No one asks you to supply a lyric or take a verse. The song remains with those who want to sing, and the meal carries on around it.

turns.input: When the meal is over I say goodnight and go back to my room, leaving everyone else to their plans.
turns.output:
When the last pudding bowls are cleared, the table’s conversation separates into smaller strands. Rashid and Ashara compare tomorrow’s schedules. Caelindra continues objecting to the ferryman song’s missing cook, while Seraphel taps its chorus against the table.

You rise and say, “Goodnight.”

“Goodnight, Garvey,” Rashid answers.

Ysolde and Thessaly return the farewell. Aldric wishes you a restful night. Ashara lifts her cup, and Seraphel gives you a small wave rather than forcing a rhyme into the moment.

You cross the common room and climb the stairs. Behind you, the song dispute resumes without requiring your presence.

Your room is dark except for silent lightning beyond the window. It briefly illuminates the made bed, the desk, and the framed Garvey letter on the wall before fading back into the storm.

You close the door, leaving the rest of the house to its evening.

turns.input: The following morning I ask in the library which publicly available records describe the human seat's last active years. I would like to look at the original records if they are open to students.
turns.output:
The library is quiet the following morning. Professor Stone is again at the central desk, working through a ledger beneath a pair of shaded lamps.

You ask, “Which publicly available records describe the human seat’s last active years? I’d like to look at the original records if they’re open to students.”

Stone’s pen stops. His eyes move briefly from your face to the Garvey signet before he closes the ledger.

“The open collection contains official abstracts, published addresses, and an index of petitions submitted by the final human delegation.” His answer becomes more formal than it was when he helped you find the Council primer. “The original correspondence, working drafts, and unabridged committee minutes are restricted. Students require the chancellor’s signature for each requested collection.”

He indicates a tall glass-fronted cabinet beneath the gallery. Its brass lock bears the Academy seal.

“The public index is still useful. It records documents excluded from the abstracts, even when it cannot give you their contents.”

Stone leads you to the historical shelves and removes three volumes. The first is a set of official Council summaries from the final decade before the human collapse. The second is titled *Petitions and Arbitrations of the Human Delegation: A Public Index*. The third contains selected speeches by Dan Garvey, identified in its frontispiece as the last active human Council representative.

“The summaries omit failed motions and most private deliberation,” Stone says. “Use the index beside them. A missing text may still have a date, submitting office, and subject.”

He places the books on an open reading table.

“If you decide to request an original, the catalogue entry will give you its collection number. The access form is held in the chancellor’s office.”

Stone returns to his desk. Before reopening his ledger, he aligns the same small stack of catalogue cards twice. The three public volumes remain available before you.
